facts.fact: 开场由叙述者回忆交代：François 生前住在 Mark 与叙述者公寓的对门，是他们在这座城市里共同交到的第一个朋友（「across the hall from Mark and me」／「the first friend we shared in the city」）。
facts.anchor: across the hall from Mark and me. He was our friend, the first friend we shared in the city.

facts.fact: François 原在一所招收早慧儿童的上西区私立学校当美术教师，用法语口音与品味冒充教学资历；他病相明显后，校董会以他的脸『吓到孩子们』为由要求他辞职——他此前一直小心用化妆遮盖 KS，甚至自认没人看破（「He used to be an art teacher at a private school」／「the school board asked him to resign」／「no one else noticed」）。
facts.anchor: He used to be an art teacher at a private school for precocious Upper West Side children, passing off his French accent and sense of style as the equivalent of a teaching degree. His walls were filled with his students’ drawings, all crayon and primary colors. “They’re better than any shit at the gallery on the corner,” he’d say. “Any child can scribble on a wall. Of course, I am not jealous.” Springtime of last year, once he really started looking sick, the school board asked him to resign because, they said, his face was “scaring the children.” He had been taking such care to cover his KS with makeup that I actually think he convinced himself that no one else noticed.

facts.fact: 他气得打碎了两面手镜；叙述者问他一共有几面手镜，他挥手把问题打发掉；他随后撕掉墙上每一张学生画作与每一串歪斜的纸娃娃；叙述者提议一同诅咒背后捅刀的校董会与那些护着『小天使』的家长，同时还得先弄清他失去医保后怎么办；他反复说『这不可能』；于是两人在走廊的污水槽里烧掉这些画作，并外加他用红色马克笔画的一张敌人漫画像（「I broke two of my hand mirrors」／「count that high」／「He tore down every construction paper drawing」／「the backstabbing school board」／「the slop sink in the hall」／「he drew with a red marker」）。
facts.anchor:
I broke two of my hand mirrors.”


I asked him how many hand mirrors he had, and he waved the question away, as if it were impossible to count that high.


He tore down every construction paper drawing, every last series of lopsided paper dolls holding hands. I suggested we plot ways to curse the backstabbing school board and the parents who worried for their precious little angels, right after we figured out what he’d do without health insurance, which, for a French person, was an inconceivable problem. It’s not possible, he kept saying. A thing about François is he liked to say things were a catastrophe. Missing the train, spilling his coffee, coming down with a cold before a hot date. But when he got really sick, he didn’t call it a catastrophe. He just said, “It’s not possible” over and over, like he could ward off the worst with it. So we burned the art in the slop sink in the hall, along with a caricature of his enemies he drew with a red marker.

facts.fact: 烧画后他不再化妆，因为意识到吓人的是他的愤怒而不是他的脸；他越病越拥抱愤怒，先说愤怒让他好受、后说愤怒让他活着；但 Mark 看着难受，把看他变糟比作列车尖叫冲来时被人从站台边拽回——即使庆幸，也忍不住想象身体被碾碎；François 的衰退一波波推进：牙龈 KS、中风、脑部病变、失明、痴呆（「After that, he stopped with the makeup」／「it kept him alive」／「It upset Mark, though」／「blindness, dementia」）。
facts.anchor:
After that, he stopped with the makeup, having realized that it was his anger more than his face that scared people. The sicker he got, the more he embraced that anger. At first, he said his anger made him feel better, and later he said it kept him alive.


It upset Mark, though. He said that watching François get worse felt like getting pulled away from the edge of a platform when a train was screaming toward you. Even if you were glad to be spared, you couldn’t help but picture your body crushed.


François’s decline came in waves: KS on his gums, stroke, brain lesions, blindness, dementia.

facts.fact: 他认为所有人最终都会得病、只需一点坏运气：会先卷过同性恋、再卷过异性恋，也许整个腐朽的星球都会灭绝；被问『女同性恋呢』时他答除非她们是往自己身上打针的坏女孩，好女孩可以留下来照顾剩下的孩子（叙述者回『滚』）；他也怨恨那些会活下来的人，认定他们会觉得自己更强或更有德，而他『太坏』（「thought everyone would get it eventually」／「Even the lesbians」／「and I am so bad」）。
facts.anchor:
thought everyone would get it eventually, that all it took was a little bad luck, that it would rip through the gays and then the straights, and then maybe the whole rotten planet would die out.


“Even the lesbians?” I asked.


“Perhaps not,” he said. “Unless they are very bad girls who inject themselves with needles. The good ones can take care of the children who remain.”


“Fuck off,” I said. “Absolutely not.”


He had been bitter about those who would survive. “Everyone who lives longer than me,” he said, scowling, “will think it is because they are stronger. Or more virtuous. They didn’t visit the bathhouses, they didn’t have too many partners. They were good, and I am so bad.

facts.fact: 他想回法国治疗，笃信那里不会像这里一样把他当垃圾；男友 Leon 说『在这个国家，垃圾是会有人处理的』，Mark 接话说垃圾工每隔几年就罢工一次，François 嘶了一声；叙述者说该让 Teamsters 接手、年底就有解药，Leon 又拿 May 68 调侃他（「He wanted to go home to France for treatment」／「garbage gets taken care of」／「go on strike every couple of years」／「As is their right」／「get the Teamsters on it」／「part of May」）。
facts.anchor:
He wanted to go home to France for treatment because, he was sure, they wouldn’t treat him like garbage like they did here. His boyfriend, Leon, said, “Don’t be silly, baby. In this country, garbage gets taken care of.”


“It’s a good line,” Mark said. “But the garbagemen do go on strike every couple of years.”


“As is their right,” François said with a hiss.

facts.fact: 他清早七点去社区健康中心开会、接热线电话、跑募款、参加 GMHC 会议（当时他躯干上还缠着带状疱疹）；被叫『受害者』他会朝你扔东西；他越病越怒、也越像他自己，但心智越来越浑浊，直到愤怒吞掉他、他失去控制：走廊里失禁、尖叫、朝不敢碰他的医护吐口水；他在政府宣布艾滋病由病毒引起、两年内会有疫苗的那天陷入昏迷，Leon 把消息耳语进他耳朵，他若听懂也没有高兴地醒来（「went to meetings at the Community Health Center」／「answered calls on the hotline」／「went to the fundraisers」／「the GMHC meetings」／「If you called him a victim」／「He slumped into a coma」／「wake up happy」）。
facts.anchor: went to meetings at the Community Health Center at seven in the morning, answered calls on the hotline, went to the fundraisers, went to the GMHC meetings where, he said, doctors and social workers told him what it was like to have AIDS while he had shingles zipping up his torso. If you called him a victim, he’d throw something at you. As he got sicker, he got angrier, angrier, somehow more himself in his anger, and as a year passed with no response from anyone with power, and the groups he organized with fought and fractured, and as his anger got stronger, his mind got cloudier until the anger swallowed him and he lost all control, dribbling shit as he walked down the hall, screaming, spitting at the people in the hospital who were too afraid to touch him. He slumped into a coma the day the government announced that AIDS was caused by a virus and they’d have a vaccine in two years. Leon whispered the news into François’s ear, but if he understood, he didn’t wake up happy.

facts.fact: 叙述者说最让他害怕的是人能那样一路拖下去、死后仍能感觉到被丢下等死的折磨——François 的愤怒比他活得更久；François 从叙述者公寓消失后，叙述者仍感觉到他在身旁：空气重新发闷却带静电，水像狗碗里的水一样走味，他裹上所有毯子压着湿毛巾，一直躺到天亮，盼光让他敢起身（「I think what frightened me more than anything」／「His anger outlived him」／「vanished from my apartment」／「like a dog bowl」／「wrapped myself in every blanket」／「safe enough to get up」）。
facts.anchor:
I think what frightened me more than anything was knowing that someone could go on that way, that even after you were dead, you could still feel the hell of being left to die. His anger outlived him.


After François vanished from my apartment, I still felt him with me. The air was stuffy again, but staticky, the way it is when it storms but the humidity isn’t burned off by lightning. I thought of getting back into the tub, but the water felt stale, like a dog bowl. I staggered to bed, wrapped myself in every blanket I had over my damp towel, and didn’t move until dawn, when the light, I hoped, would make me feel safe enough to get up.
